title: Why Your Website Gets Traffic But No Enquiries
excerpt: Traffic without enquiries is a conversion problem, not a traffic problem. Here are the most common reasons your website visitors aren't contacting you.

blocks.text: You check your analytics. The traffic numbers look reasonable — maybe even good. But the phone isn't ringing and the enquiry form isn't filling up.
This is one of the most frustrating positions to be in as a business owner. You've done the hard work of getting people to your site. They're arriving. They're just not doing anything.
Traffic without conversion is a specific problem with specific causes. Here are the most common ones — and what to do about each.
1. Your Call to Action Is Missing or Buried
The single most common reason websites don't generate enquiries: there is no clear, prominent call to action telling visitors what to do next.
Check your homepage on a phone. Without scrolling, can you see a button or link telling you to call, book, or enquire? If not — that's your first fix.
A CTA that works:

items: Is visible above the fold (before any scrolling) on mobile
Uses action language: 'Get a quote', 'Book a free call', 'Contact us today'
Appears on every page — not just the contact page
Stands out visually from the rest of the page (contrasting colour, clear button)

blocks.text: If your CTA is a small grey link in the footer, it might as well not exist.
2. You're Attracting the Wrong Visitors
Not all traffic is equal. A thousand visitors who are casually curious about your industry are worth less than ten visitors who are actively looking to hire someone like you.

If your site ranks for broad informational keywords — 'what is SEO', 'how does web design work' — you'll get traffic from people researching, not buying. That traffic will never convert well, because it was never the right traffic.
High-converting traffic comes from buyer-intent keywords:

items: 'web design agency [city]'
'wordpress to nextjs migration service'
'fast website for small business'
'hire web developer for business site'

blocks.text: Check your Search Console to see which queries are bringing people to your site. If the terms are all informational, your content strategy needs to shift toward purchase-intent pages.
3. Visitors Don't Trust You Yet
Someone arrives at your website. They don't know you. Within 10–15 seconds, they're deciding whether you're credible enough to contact.
Most business websites fail this test. They have no social proof, no specific results, no faces, and no evidence that anyone has worked with them before.
Trust signals that actually move the needle:

items: Client testimonials with full names and companies (not anonymous 'John D.')
Logos of recognisable clients or partners
Specific results: 'Site speed improved from 42 to 96', '30% more enquiries in 3 months'
A photo of you or your team — people buy from people
Number of clients served, years in business, or other credibility signals

blocks.text: If your homepage says 'We deliver quality solutions for your business needs', you sound like every other agency. If it says 'We've migrated 47 WordPress sites to Next.js, with an average PageSpeed improvement of 45 points', you're different.
4. Your Copy Talks About You, Not the Reader
Read your homepage copy. Count how many times it uses 'we', 'our', 'us' versus 'you' and 'your'.

Most business websites are written from the seller's perspective. 'We are a full-service digital agency with 10 years of experience delivering innovative solutions...' This is not what a potential client is thinking about.
A potential client is thinking: 'My website is slow and I'm losing customers. Can these people fix it? How quickly? What will it cost?'
Effective copy leads with the reader's problem, not your credentials:

items: 'Your WordPress site is costing you customers. Here's how to fix it.'
'Most business websites score 45 on PageSpeed. Yours could score 95.'
'Stop paying for plugins. Stop worrying about updates. Focus on your business.'

blocks.text: The rule: every sentence on your homepage should either address the reader's problem, demonstrate you can solve it, or tell them what to do next.
5. Your Site Is Too Slow
A slow website doesn't just hurt your SEO rankings — it kills conversions directly.
Google's data: a 1-second delay in mobile load time reduces conversions by up to 20%. A site that takes 5 seconds to load loses roughly half its visitors before they've seen anything.
The average WordPress site on shared hosting takes 3–6 seconds to load on mobile. Your visitors decide whether to stay or go in about 3 seconds. Do the maths.
Check your mobile PageSpeed score at pagespeed.web.dev. If you're below 60, speed is almost certainly a contributing factor to your low conversion rate.
Speed improvements that have the biggest impact on conversions: faster server response time, optimised images, removing unused JavaScript, and moving to a static or server-rendered architecture.
6. The Contact Process Has Too Much Friction
Someone decides they want to contact you. What happens next?
If the answer is 'they have to find the contact page, fill in 8 fields including company size and annual budget, then wait for a callback', you've built a wall between you and your leads.
The lower the friction, the more enquiries you get. This means:

items: Contact forms with the minimum number of fields (name, email, message is usually enough)
A direct phone number that works, visible on every page
A direct email address — not just a form
A booking link if relevant (Calendly, Cal.com) for people who prefer to schedule immediately
Responding quickly — slow responses teach people that contacting you isn't worth it

blocks.text: If your form asks for a budget, project timeline, company size, and how they heard about you before letting someone send a message — you're losing people to that friction.
7. You Haven't Addressed the Obvious Objections
Every potential client who visits your site has questions they're not asking. They want to know: How much does it cost? How long will it take? What if I'm not happy with the result?
If your website doesn't answer these questions, visitors will make up their own answers — and those invented answers are almost always worse than reality.
You don't need exact prices if your work is custom. But you need ballpark figures. 'Projects typically start at €1,500' is more reassuring than silence, because it lets people self-qualify.
Common objections to address on your site:

items: Cost: at least a price range or starting point
Timeline: typical project length
Process: what working with you looks like, step by step
Risk: what happens if they're not happy, guarantees, or refund policy
Fit: who is this service for, and who is it not for

blocks.text: 8. Your Mobile Experience Is Broken

More than 60% of your visitors are on a phone. If the mobile experience is poor — text too small, buttons too close together, images overflowing, navigation not working — you're quietly losing the majority of your traffic.
Test your own site on a phone right now. Try to find the contact form. Try to read the main paragraph. Try to tap the primary CTA button.
If any of these is annoying or difficult, fix it. A broken mobile experience is one of the most reliably damaging conversion problems — and also one of the most fixable.
9. There's Nothing to Capture Interest Before They're Ready to Buy
Most visitors aren't ready to enquire on their first visit. They're researching. They'll come back when they're ready — but only if they remember you.
Without a way to capture their email or stay in touch, you're leaving warm leads to go cold. They'll visit three other providers, forget your name, and enquire with whoever is freshest in their mind.
Options to capture interest before a visitor is ready to buy:

items: A free tool or resource relevant to your audience (a template, a calculator, a checklist)
A newsletter with useful content, not just promotions
A lead magnet — something of genuine value in exchange for an email address
Retargeting ads that keep you visible after someone leaves your site

blocks.text: Even a simple 'Get our free website checklist' sign-up can capture the 80% of visitors who weren't ready to enquire on the first visit.
10. You Haven't Told Visitors What to Do Next
Every page on your website should end with a clear next step. Not just a contact page link — an explicit instruction.
Most websites end their pages with nothing. The visitor reads the content, feels vaguely interested, and then... leaves, because there was no prompt to do anything else.

The fix is straightforward: end every service page, blog post, and about page with a specific CTA. Not 'Contact us' in the footer. A sentence like: 'If your site scores below 60 on PageSpeed, we can fix that. Book a free 20-minute call and we'll tell you exactly what's holding it back.'
Specific, direct, with a clear value proposition. That's what converts.
Where to Start
If you're overwhelmed by the list above, start with these three:

items: **Visible CTA above the fold on mobile.** This is the highest-impact single change most businesses can make.
**At least one testimonial with a real name on the homepage.** Trust is the most common invisible barrier.
**Check your PageSpeed score.** If you're below 60, speed is costing you conversions.

blocks.text: Fix these three first. Then work through the rest.
